Your browser does not support the video element. DesktopPet is a cat that lives on the macOS desktop. Clicking it opens a chat bubble, selecting an English word in any app shows its definition and adds it to a vocabulary list, and during an English lecture or talk it turns the audio into live captions and, once the session is over, writes the whole thing up as notes in Chinese. The project is open source on GitHub. Most of the code was written by AI coding agents such as Claude Code, while my part was defining the requirements and interactions, testing it through everyday use, and comparing and choosing the models for each stage.
Why I built it Since I started my master’s abroad, almost all of my classes, talks and online meetings have been in English, and in class I often have several tools open at once: captions for the parts I can’t catch, a dictionary for unfamiliar words, and later the recording so I can go back and write notes. Products like Feishu Minutes already handle much of this well, but the features are spread across different windows and switching between them keeps breaking my concentration, and I was also curious how well locally deployed models would actually work.
What I wanted was a single entry point that stays on top of the desktop and can be called up at any time, with the tools I need for studying gathered in one place. For the character I used a silver-shaded British Shorthair I used to have, since a small cat that keeps you company is something people are far more willing to leave on screen all day than a tool panel. My original brief had only three items: a pinned desktop pet you can chat with, translation and a vocabulary list for English words that are typed or selected, and streaming captions while an English video plays. Before anything was built, I asked for a survey of existing open-source projects that could be adapted easily, and the plan was based on that.
Narrowing the scope first The first version was adapted from an open-source virtual-avatar project that came with a lot of extras, including a character persona, text-to-speech, Live2D models and several window modes. Since the pet was meant for studying, I didn’t want features that had nothing to do with studying competing for attention, so I removed the persona and TTS and kept only the pet itself, chat and word lookup, leaving captions for the next step.
Removing the persona turned up an interesting problem. The prototype had a persona written from a config template, a character called “Naitang”, and even after it was deleted the name kept appearing in replies. It turned out the cause was my assistant’s memory store, which mixed two kinds of entries: dated event logs recording what happened at the time, which are harmless to keep, and profile entries describing the current state, which were correct when they were written but had never been updated along with the project. One of them still said “currently using the Naitang persona”, so it kept being pulled back in during retrieval. The fix was to keep the event logs and update the profile entries, and it made me realise that history and current state need to be managed separately in long-term memory, because old records do no harm, while a current state that isn’t kept up to date quietly becomes wrong information after a while.
Whether it stays open depends on the details For a tool that lives on the desktop all day, how comfortable it feels depends much more on details such as focus, input methods, bubble placement, screen edges and animation timing than on how many features it has. After using it for a while, most of my change requests were about exactly these things. The chat bubble should follow the cat, flip direction according to which corner of the screen the cat is in and always stay inside the screen; clicking the cat opens or closes the bubble and clicking anywhere else dismisses it; the input field is focused as soon as the bubble opens, messages are sent with Enter, and there is neither a send button nor a close button; the candidate window of the Chinese input method must never be hidden behind the bubble; and the cat can be dragged onto an external display but never somewhere it can’t be found again, starting on the main screen by default.
Clicking the cat opens the chat bubble with the input field already focused; press Enter to send, with buttons below for captions, conversations and the vocabulary list
I based the cat’s timing on a real cat as well. When nobody is paying attention it sleeps, a click makes it get up, wink and sit, and about five seconds after the bubble closes it yawns before eventually lying back down to sleep. The acceptance criterion for captions also came from the reading experience, which is that in the same video the pauses in the captions should never fall in the middle of a sentence.
The vocabulary list, where every looked-up word is kept for review or removal
Captions: two scenarios, with models chosen per stage Captions took more time than anything else in this project, and they also gave me a much more concrete sense of what local models can do.
Along the way I realised there are really two different scenarios here. Live captions for online meetings and lectures need very low latency, so the model has to support streaming output, whereas captioning an existing recording or video can tolerate some delay but has to process the whole piece in one go, which makes accuracy more important.
The first implementation cut the audio into fixed-length chunks and passed them to Whisper, so the captions only appeared in bursts about every six seconds and felt choppy to read. I then compared macOS’s built-in SpeechAnalyzer with Whisper large-v3 on the same lecture recording. SpeechAnalyzer refreshed about once a second and was 7 to 11 times faster, but it gives up understanding for speed: without broader context it can only guess from the current sentence, it was worse with technical terms, and giving it a glossary made no measurable difference.
So in the end I didn’t pick a single model but split the work into stages. This is the local setup I use every day:
Stage Setup Reason Live captions in class Apple SpeechAnalyzer, from either the microphone or system audio, with the recording saved It was the only option with low enough latency Re-transcription after class Claude Sonnet first extracts a glossary from the live captions, then a local Qwen3-ASR re-transcribes the recording using that glossary In a 106-minute lecture with 8 terms known to be misrecognised, Qwen3-ASR got 7 right and Apple got 1 Class notes Sonnet reads the full transcript and writes notes in Chinese, then code checks every quote and timestamp Batch summaries from small local models weren’t good enough The split was mainly about saving tokens, with repetitive, mechanical and high-volume work going to local models and work that requires reading the whole transcript and understanding context going to a large cloud model. Where model output couldn’t be trusted, I tried two kinds of guardrails. The code guardrail checks that every quote in the notes can be found in the original transcript and that its timestamp matches, and the small-model guardrail uses a small model for term correction, where Qwen 4B produced the same corrections as 9B at roughly three times the speed. For one 68-minute talk, all 41 quotes and 209 timestamps in the generated notes passed the checks.
All of these models were chosen by comparing their outputs directly on the same material, and I mainly looked at three things: size and performance, meaning whether my machine could handle the model and whether it was fast enough; structured output and instruction following, meaning whether it produced properly formatted captions or leaked the prompt into them; and recognition quality, including how much it hallucinated on background noise and how well it handled technical terms, numbers and formulas.
What isn’t good enough yet: the animation I want the pet to look lifelike and move smoothly, and it isn’t there yet. I’ve tried several approaches and each has its own problem. The pets bundled with Codex and Hermes are low resolution, so the cat’s fur loses its texture; GIFs have a limited number of colours, which hurts the fur in the same way; and generating a video and then extracting frames is a lot of work and makes it hard to control the pet’s movements precisely, so an interaction like the cat stopping mid-run when clicked and turning to look at you would be difficult to pull off.
The current approach generates each frame with GPT and stitches the frames together in code. Each individual frame looks good, but GPT can’t keep frames aligned with each other, and the edges of the generated images shift slightly from one to the next, so the motion stutters when they’re played in sequence.
Working with AI Almost all of the code in this project was written by AI coding agents. My job was to define the requirements and acceptance criteria, find problems through daily use, make the trade-offs, judge the results of the model comparisons and take responsibility for how the final product works. Partway through, the project was rewritten as a native macOS app, and before the rewrite the key behaviours were recorded as 20 regression cases so that the new version could be checked against them one by one instead of being accepted because it “looks about the same”.
The open-source version currently needs macOS 26 or later on Apple Silicon and connects by default to any OpenAI-compatible API, including a local Ollama or LM Studio. The “Qwen3-ASR re-transcription plus Sonnet notes” pipeline described above is my own local configuration and isn’t part of the open-source version’s default features.
The video at the top was also made with code: the visuals are 2D animation written in HTML and rendered frame by frame, and the background music was synthesised by a program.
summary: A study companion that lives on the macOS desktop, with chat, word lookup, live captions and notes after class. This post covers the scope decisions, the model comparisons and a few things I learned along the way.
title: DesktopPet: A Desktop Pet I Built to Help Me Study in English

Deploying OpenClaw Server and system setup Tencent Cloud Lighthouse instance: 4 CPU cores, 4GB RAM, 70GB system disk
Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS 64-bit — ChatGPT recommended this as the most compatible option.
Installing OpenClaw Update the system and install dependencies # Update the system sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y # Install base dependencies sudo apt install -y git curl wget unzip build-essential # Install nvm curl -o- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.39.7/install.sh | bash source ~/.bashrc # Install Node.js nvm install --lts nvm use --lts # Verify the install and check versions node -v npm -v Install OpenClaw npm install -g openclaw@latest Start OpenClaw # Initialise config and install openclaw onboard --install-daemon # install-daemon registers the OpenClaw Gateway as a background daemon: it runs # silently, starts on boot, and restarts itself if it crashes From ChatGPT:
Setting What it means What it does Recommendation How to configure it if you skip it model / auth provider Choose your model provider and how you authenticate Determines which models are available, how they’re called, cost, and latency Pick the strongest model you have access to, or the most reliable provider — OpenAI / Anthropic / Ollama Fill it in later via openclaw configure or by editing models.providers directly filter models by provider Filter models down to one provider Keeps the model list manageable and avoids picking something unsupported Beginners: stick to one provider. Advanced users: filter precisely Use openclaw models list + openclaw models set <model>, or edit the config file default model The model used by default Determines which model the agent calls as its primary Set a strong model as primary and a cheaper one as fallback Set manually: openclaw models set <model>, or edit agents.defaults.model.primary model check Checks that the model is reachable Verifies the API key is valid and the provider is up Do this — it’s the only way to be sure the agent will actually work Run manually: openclaw models status select channel Choose the bot’s entry channel Determines how users interact with the agent Telegram/Discord/Web/UI — use Web/CLI for local testing, Telegram or Docker + channel for production Configure later via openclaw configure or the channels config web search Whether to enable web search Lets the agent look up current information instead of relying only on training data Turn it on for an assistant or anything that needs current info; turn it off in an air-gapped environment Add a search tool later via the tools config search provider Choose a search engine Affects search quality, result structure, and cost Prefer a stable API, e.g. SerpAPI Add it later via tool config or openclaw configure hooks Lifecycle hooks Lets you inject custom logic — safety checks, logging, tool permissions Beginners can skip this; required for security/enterprise setups Add later by writing a plugin or editing the gateway config How do you want to hatch your bot? Determines how the agent gets initialized Controls the creation flow and configuration complexity Pick TUI — the two don’t conflict, the web UI is still reachable, but the TUI won’t be interactive until an LLM API is configured Re-run openclaw onboard later, or edit the config manually Accessing the web UI remotely Run this on your local machine’s command line, then open 127.0.0.1:18789 in your browser.
My first impression of the web UI for configuration wasn’t great — it’s clearly built for developers, not for casual users. The settings aren’t self-explanatory and there’s no inline help — for example, to configure the LLM API you have to type raw JSON into a text box, with no documentation on the expected format anywhere in sight. The TUI is honestly much easier to use.
# Open an SSH local port-forwarding tunnel, so a service running on the remote # server is reachable from your own machine over the encrypted SSH channel. ssh -N -L 18789:127.0.0.1:18789 your-username@your-server-ip Configuring the LLM API # Configuration command openclaw configure https://bailian.console.aliyun.com/cn-beijing/?spm=5176.45613825.0.0.46735b4cFCNR9w&tab=doc#/doc/?type=model&url=3020785
Setting up the QQ bot — chatting with “the lobster” over QQ Sessions are isolated by entry point and session instance — the TUI and QQ chat are two separate main sessions, and they don’t share context or memory.
https://q.qq.com/qqbot/openclaw/
Setting up the agent First contact: bootstrapping Inside .openclaw/workspace there’s a BOOTSTRAP.md file. The first time you talk to the agent through the TUI, the LLM reads this file first, follows its instructions to work out who it’s supposed to be through the conversation, then rewrites files like agent.md and deletes BOOTSTRAP.md.
Worth noting: talking to the agent directly through the QQ bot does NOT trigger bootstrapping — you need to go through the TUI or the web UI for that.
Key configuration areas Control layer — how it thinks ├── SOUL.md ├── model config Memory layer — what it remembers ├── session (short-term) ├── memory (long-term) ├── RAG (external) Execution layer — how it gets things done ├── workspace ├── tools ├── skills ├── sub-agents Setting What it does Session-isolated? Persistent? Affects tokens? Typical use workspace The agent’s working directory — files, code, run artifacts Yes Yes No (indirectly) File handling, code execution, task output SOUL.md / AGENT.md The agent’s core behavior rules (system prompt) No (injected globally) Yes Yes (heavy) Controls the agent’s strategy, persona, and how it executes memory Long-term storage (structured or unstructured) Depends on config Yes Yes (moderate) Remembering user preferences, historical info session (main conversation) The current conversation context Yes No (short-lived) Yes (heavy) Multi-turn dialogue, contextual reasoning sub-agent session A sub-agent’s own independent execution context Yes (fully isolated) No Yes (light) Running complex or long-running tasks compaction Summarizing/compressing a long context Yes No Yes (reduces usage) Keeping context length under control, saving tokens tools The set of tools the agent can call No (global config) Yes No Doing things externally — API calls, running code skills Pre-packaged higher-level capabilities (tool combos) No Yes No Reusable capabilities, e.g. a task workflow model config Model parameters (maxTokens, temperature, etc.) No Yes Yes (heavy) Controls generation behavior and cost RAG / embeddings External knowledge retrieval No (usually global) Yes Yes (moderate) Supplying long-term knowledge Mechanism Trigger Time-dependent? Runs in the main session? Has context? Creates a task record? Key trait Typical use cron job Time-based (exact time / cron expression) Yes (exact) Optional (main / isolated) Optional (none if isolated) Yes Precise scheduling, can run isolated Scheduled reports, reminders, batch jobs heartbeat Fixed interval (default 30 minutes) Yes (approximate) Yes (main session) Yes (full context) No Periodic “check-in / think” Inbox checks, notifications, status monitoring hook Event-triggered (lifecycle events, tool calls, etc.) No Depends on the event Depends No Event-driven, immediate Automation, intercepting/enhancing behavior If there’s nothing that needs the agent to periodically check on its own, turn off heartbeat to save tokens. cron = I tell it when to act heartbeat = it periodically checks in on its own hook = something happens, it reacts automatically Sub-agents and multi-agent setups You can set up the main agent to spin off a sub-agent for complex, time-consuming tasks, and have it report the result back — which saves both tokens and time.
Sub-agents are non-blocking: the main agent doesn’t wait for them and can keep talking to the user, and once the sub-agent finishes, it reports its result back and the loop closes. A sub-agent runs in its own session and doesn’t inherit the main agent’s context or SOUL.md, which is what saves tokens. Think of a sub-agent as a temp worker: it runs its task in the background and hands the result back once it’s done. Good fit for long tasks, parallel tasks, and specialized work. You configure SOUL.md to tell the main agent when to spin up a sub-agent, and give the sub-agent its own prompt to define its identity and rules so it can do its specific job well.
You can also run multiple long-lived agents in parallel, each with its own workspace, memory, SOUL.md, and session.
Useful for setting up multiple long-term “personas” — one that only writes code, one that only does research — each with its own memory and identity. Each can have different permissions, different models, and different messaging channels (WeChat vs. QQ). Context window settings My first impression: this thing burns through tokens fast. Even a simple exchange can cost tens of thousands of tokens, and if you’re using a weaker LLM that gets stuck in a reasoning loop, token usage can spike into the millions for a single hard task.
Set the context window size based on what the model can actually handle — for example, MiniMax 2.5 natively supports a 200k context window. A bigger context window makes the conversation flow better and cuts down on how often the system needs to compress information.
Trying out skills Time management with a Notion database https://clawhub.ai/xiangtaoxiao/notion-time-management-matrix
I built this on top of a Notion database template I’d already made (a four-quadrant time management matrix) as the data source, with OpenClaw hitting it through the Notion API. You add or close to-dos over WeChat chat, get automatic reminders as deadlines approach, and can pull related files/info and update progress on a task. See the Notion skill docs for the actual API calls.
What’s better about this than the traditional way of doing it? Chatting over WeChat feels a lot more natural, and an AI assistant can add a bit of emotional warmth to it too 🐶 Honestly, just keeping everything inside OpenClaw itself works the best functionally — the trade-off is you lose a nice-looking interface, and you need to guard against the LLM being flaky and corrupting your data. You can use OpenClaw’s own cron jobs to periodically check to-dos and send reminders. Under the hood, cron is just firing off an instruction to the AI through a specific session at a specific time. Problems I ran into TRAE doesn’t follow OpenClaw’s conventions: fixed it by giving the agent a link to the OpenClaw skill docs and having it read them. After installing the skill, the agent didn’t pick it up: added a prompt in TOOL.md telling the AI explicitly to use this skill, and also explicitly asked for it on the first message of a conversation. As for why the agent doesn’t automatically trigger the skill by semantic matching once it’s installed — my guess is OpenClaw’s system prompt or the agent’s own prompt already has a default way of handling to-dos baked in, and that takes priority. Skill status shows “not ready”: run the command below to see which requirement isn’t met, then fix it. openclaw skills check Hard to debug — no visibility into the agent’s reasoning or tool calls: installed Clawmetry to fix this. The system mangled a path — extra spaces, wrong characters — so the command wouldn’t run. I asked GPT and made two fixes: renamed the skill’s folder to swap - for _, and added ./script/ to the path in the prompt. After that it worked cleanly — the AI didn’t need to retry, it just ran successfully. The AI’s task logic isn’t always very rigorous — I ran into a case where it acted purely from memory instead of reading the actual status file. In theory that’s the “smart” move, but if the prompt doesn’t require it, the AI won’t reliably notice when things have changed. (This was with MiniMax 2.5.) OpenClaw’s built-in memory isn’t great — right now the memory file has picked up a lot of unimportant, even outright wrong, content, and it’s badly polluting the context. Sometimes even when I explicitly point out an error and ask it to remember the correction, it still doesn’t get written to the memory file. Maybe worth trying calling the Notion API directly (i.e. the Notion skill) and customizing it so the AI understands what each database is for and how it’s structured — could that get me synced to-do and knowledge-base management? Lessons learned Prompt tricks that worked:
Stop the AI from improvising: point it at the official docs and have it read them first, then explicitly forbid it from deviating from what the docs specify. Stop the AI from only fixing things locally instead of thinking about the whole picture. Work around some models being bad at handling tokens like - and at concatenating instructions correctly: different models — and different temperature settings — vary a lot in how reliably they build paths and system commands. When that’s unstable, it’s better to hard-code the command as a tool and have the AI just call the tool with its output. This will probably get better as LLMs improve. Stop the AI from always acting on memory: OpenClaw does have a memory structure, but if some key piece of data changes and the AI still acts on what it remembers instead of the current state, that leads to failures or corrupted updates. For anything that’s a critical setting, it’s better to require the AI to read the actual config file rather than pull it from context or memory — especially while debugging.

AI Agents, From Chatbot to Production An AI agent is the LLM application taken further — something that can plan on its own, carry out tasks, and interact with its environment.
Foundational papers:
Yao, S., et al. (2022). “ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models.” ICLR. [paper] — the ReAct framework, the core pattern behind most agents Wei, J., et al. (2022). “Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models.” NeurIPS. [paper] Wang, G., et al. (2024). “A Survey on Large Language Model based Autonomous Agents.” arXiv. [paper] — a survey of the agent landscape 1. The Overall Progression Chatbot → Tool Use → Agent → Production Agent What each stage means:
Chatbot: can only talk, can’t take any action in the outside world Tool Use: can call a single tool Agent: can plan and carry out multi-step tasks on its own Production Agent: the industrial-strength version — error handling, permission control, monitoring, all of it 2. Breaking Down the Core Concepts 2.1 Chatbot LLM + Prompt
What defines it:
can only converse can’t take any external action no state, or only weak state Foundational paper:
Vinyals, O., & Le, Q. (2015). “A Neural Conversational Model.” ICML Deep Learning Workshop. [paper] 2.2 Function / Tool / Function Calling Function The smallest unit of code that actually does something.
Tool The LLM-facing description of a function — what it’s called, what it expects, what it does.
Foundational papers:
Schick, T., et al. (2023). “Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.” NeurIPS. [paper] — the foundational work on tool learning Parisi, A., et al. (2022). “TALM: Tool Augmented Language Models.” arXiv. [paper] Function calling The LLM produces a structured call request, and the runtime executes it.
How it’s implemented in practice:
OpenAI’s Function Calling API Anthropic’s Tool Use LangChain Tools 3. What an Agent Actually Is LLM + Tools + a Loop
Foundational papers:
Yao, S., et al. (2022). “ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models.” ICLR. [paper] Shinn, N., et al. (2023). “Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning.” NeurIPS. [paper] The Agent loop Thought → Action → Observation → Thought... A worked example from the ReAct paper:
Question: What is the elevation range for the area that the eastern sector of the Colorado orogeny extends into? Thought 1: I need to search Colorado orogeny, find the area that the eastern sector of the Colorado orogeny extends into, then find the elevation range of that area. Action 1: Search[Colorado orogeny] Observation 1: The Colorado orogeny was an episode of mountain building... Thought 2: I need to search eastern sector of the Colorado orogeny. Action 2: Search[eastern sector of Colorado orogeny] ... 4. Agent Runtime The Agent Runtime is the infrastructure that actually executes an agent’s logic.
What it’s responsible for:
parsing tool calls executing the underlying function/API controlling the loop (max iterations, timeouts) error handling permission control state management Common frameworks:
LangChain AutoGPT BabyAGI CrewAI Microsoft AutoGen References:
Richards, T. (2023). “AutoGPT.” [GitHub] Nakajima, Y. (2023). “BabyAGI.” [GitHub] 5. Tool Retrieval Using embeddings to semantically match a user’s request against a large tool library, and passing the LLM only the Top-K most relevant tools.
Foundational paper:
Qin, Y., et al. (2023). “Tool Learning with Foundation Models.” arXiv. [paper] — a survey of tool learning Flow:
User question → embedding → search the tool library → Top-K tools → LLM picks one to call 6. Skill A Skill = a composed capability made up of several Tools
A Skill packages up the ability to handle a complex task — think of it as the AI equivalent of a human “skill.”
Examples:
A “write a blog post” Skill = search tool + writing tool + image generation tool A “data analysis” Skill = data query tool + visualization tool + report generation tool 7. Production Agent Architecture User → Retriever → LLM → Runtime → Tool → Observation → LLM → Response What production actually requires:
error handling and retries monitoring and logging permission control cost control security auditing 8. Principles Worth Remembering The model sets the ceiling; the runtime sets the floor.
What the model can do defines the agent’s upper bound. How solid the runtime is defines how stable and reliable the agent actually is day to day.
Retrieve before you reason.
Pull in the relevant information and tools before trying to execute the task.
Use Skills to package up complexity.
Wrap frequently-used, complex tasks into a Skill — it makes things more reusable and more reliable.
9. A Mental Model Component Analogy What it does LLM The brain Reasoning, planning, decision-making Tools Hands Carry out concrete actions Skills Muscle memory Packaged, complex capabilities Retriever Perception Pulls in information and tools Runtime Nervous system Coordinates execution, passes information around 10. Wrapping Up Agent = LLM + Tools + Loop + Runtime + Retrieval (+ Skills)
An AI agent is the LLM application pushed a step further — from a system that just talks, to one that can plan and carry out complex tasks on its own. As the underlying tech keeps improving, agents are going to keep showing up in more and more places.
References Prompt Engineering Brown, T. B., et al. (2020). “Language Models are Few-Shot Learners.” NeurIPS. Wei, J., et al. (2022). “Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models.” NeurIPS. Kojima, T., et al. (2022). “Large Language Models are Zero-Shot Reasoners.” NeurIPS. Zhou, Y., et al. (2022). “Large Language Models Are Human-Level Prompt Engineers.” ICLR. RAG Lewis, P., et al. (2020). “Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks.” NeurIPS. Guu, K., et al. (2020). “REALM: Retrieval-Augmented Language Model Pre-Training.” ICML. Karpukhin, V., et al. (2020). “Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering.” EMNLP. Prompt Engineering https://www.coursera.org/learn/chatgpt-prompt-engineering-for-developers-project/home/welcome
Prompt engineering is the practice of designing and refining the input you give a large language model so it produces the output you actually want. It took off after GPT-3 came out, and it’s basically the bridge between what a user wants and what the model can do.
Key papers:
Brown, T. B., et al. (2020). “Language Models are Few-Shot Learners.” NeurIPS. [link] — the GPT-3 paper, the first to really demonstrate the potential of prompt engineering Wei, J., et al. (2022). “Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models.” NeurIPS. [link] 1. Prompting Principles Principle 1: Write clear and specific instructions Clarity and specificity are the two things that matter most when writing a prompt. Vague instructions tend to produce unpredictable outputs, while specific ones noticeably improve output quality.
Tactic 1: Use delimiters to clearly indicate distinct parts of the input
Delimiters like ```, """, ---, or <> help the model tell different parts of your input apart, which avoids confusion — especially useful when you’re feeding in multiple chunks of text or code at once.
Tactic 2: Ask for a structured output
Asking for structured output (JSON, HTML, a Markdown table) makes the result easy to parse downstream, which is basically a best practice for building anything on top of an LLM.
Tactic 3: Ask the model to check whether conditions are satisfied
Having the model verify conditions before it acts cuts down on wrong outputs.
Tactic 4: “Few-shot” prompting — give examples
Few-shot prompting gives the model a few examples so it can pick up the format and the kind of output you expect.
Key papers:
Brown, T. B., et al. (2020). “Language Models are Few-Shot Learners.” NeurIPS. [link] — introduced the idea of few-shot learning Min, S., et al. (2022). “Rethinking the Role of Demonstrations: What Makes In-Context Learning Work?” EMNLP. [link] Principle 2: Give the model time to “think” This comes out of chain-of-thought research — letting the model reason step by step instead of jumping straight to an answer.
Key papers:
Wei, J., et al. (2022). “Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models.” NeurIPS. [link] — the paper that started it all
Kojima, T., et al. (2022). “Large Language Models are Zero-Shot Reasoners.” NeurIPS. [link] — where “let’s think step by step” comes from
Wang, X., et al. (2022). “Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models.” ICLR. [link]
Tactic 1: Specify the steps required to complete a task
Spell out the steps so the model follows them in order.
Tactic 2: Instruct the model to work out its own solution before rushing to a conclusion
Have the model work the problem out on its own before it commits to an answer, instead of guessing right away.
About Hallucinations A hallucination is when the model outputs something that sounds plausible but is actually wrong or made up.
Key papers:
Maynez, J., et al. (2020). “On Faithfulness and Factuality in Abstractive Summarization.” ACL. [link] Zhang, Y., et al. (2023). “Siren’s Song in the AI Ocean: A Survey on Hallucination in Large Language Models.” arXiv. [link] Ways to reduce it:
Ask the model to find relevant information first and answer based on that information Ask the model to cite its sources Use a RAG system to feed it reliable context 2. Iterative Prompt Development Prompt engineering is iterative — you don’t get it right the first time, you keep testing and tweaking.
Key methodology:
Zhou, Y., et al. (2022). “Large Language Models Are Human-Level Prompt Engineers.” ICLR. [link] — APE (Automatic Prompt Engineer) The loop:
Try something (write an initial prompt) Analyze where the result falls short Clarify the instructions, give the model more room to think Refine the prompt against a batch of examples 3. Summarizing Summarization is one of the most common NLP tasks, and LLMs are quite good at it.
Key papers:
See, A., et al. (2017). “Get To The Point: Summarization with Pointer-Generator Networks.” ACL. [link] Liu, Y., & Lapata, M. (2019). “Text Summarization with Pretrained Encoders.” EMNLP. [link] Things worth knowing:
Summarize with a word/sentence/character limit Summarize with a focus on a specific topic, like shipping and delivery Try “extract” instead of “summarize” when you only care about one particular topic Summarize across multiple product reviews at once 4. Inferring LLMs are pretty good at extracting specific things out of a piece of text.
They’re especially good at pulling structured information out of unstructured text.
Key paper:
Radford, A., et al. (2019). “Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners.” — the GPT-2 paper, which demonstrated zero-shot capability [link] Use cases:
Sentiment: positive or negative
Key paper: Socher, R., et al. (2013). “Recursive Deep Models for Semantic Compositionality Over a Sentiment Treebank.” EMNLP.
Identifying types of emotion: happy, grateful, angry, etc.
Key paper: Mohammad, S. M., & Turney, P. D. (2013). “Crowdsourcing a Word-Emotion Association Lexicon.” Computational Intelligence.
Identifying a specific emotion, e.g. “is the writer expressing anger?”
Extracting product and company names from customer reviews (named entity recognition)
Key paper: Nadeau, D., & Sekine, S. (2007). “A survey of named entity recognition and classification.” Lingvisticae Investigationes.
💡 Format your response as a JSON object with “Item” and “Brand” as the keys. If the information isn’t present, use “unknown” as the value. Make your response as short as possible.
Inferring topics and having the LLM answer in JSON
Key paper: Blei, D. M., Ng, A. Y., & Jordan, M. I. (2003). “Latent Dirichlet Allocation.” JMLR. — the paper that started topic modeling with LDA
Setting up a news alert for certain topics (zero-shot learning)
Key papers:
Radford, A., et al. (2021). “Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision.” ICML. — the CLIP paper [link] Xian, Y., et al. (2017). “Zero-Shot Learning - A Comprehensive Evaluation of the Good, the Bad and the Ugly.” TPAMI. [link] 5. Transforming LLMs are good at all kinds of text transformation — translation, tone shifts, format conversion, you name it.
Key paper:
Vaswani, A., et al. (2017). “Attention Is All You Need.” NeurIPS. [link] — the Transformer paper, the foundation of modern NLP Types of transformation:
Language translation
Key paper: Wu, Y., et al. (2016). “Google’s Neural Machine Translation System.” arXiv. [link]
Tone: informal to formal
Format conversion: JSON to HTML
Spelling/grammar checks, or matching a given style such as APA
Key paper: Yuan, Z., et al. (2021). “Synthesizing Coherent Story with Generative Pre-trained Transformer.” IJCAI.
6. Expanding Expanding is the opposite of summarizing — turning a short input into a longer, more detailed output.
Key paper:
Fan, A., et al. (2018). “Hierarchical Neural Story Generation.” ACL. [link] Things worth knowing:
Customize an automated reply to a customer email Remind the model to pull in details from the customer’s email Use temperature to control the answer: more creative, or more stable A note on temperature Temperature controls how random an LLM’s output is, and the idea actually comes from statistical mechanics and simulated annealing.
Key papers:
Ackley, D. H., Hinton, G. E., & Sejnowski, T. J. (1985). “A Learning Algorithm for Boltzmann Machines.” Cognitive Science. — the theoretical basis for simulated annealing Ficler, J., & Goldberg, Y. (2017). “Controlling Linguistic Style Aspects in Neural Language Generation.” EMNLP. [link] 💡 What temperature actually does is reshape the softmax probability distribution.
Temperature Effect Typical use T < 1 Sharpens the distribution (more deterministic) Stable output, good for RAG — set T = 0; many chatbots default to 0.7 T = 1 The raw distribution Standard generation T > 1 Flattens the distribution (more random) Creative writing The math behind it: $$P(x_i) = \frac{\exp(z_i/T)}{\sum_j \exp(z_j/T)}$$
7. Chatbots Chatbots are the most direct application of LLMs.
Key papers:
Vinyals, O., & Le, Q. (2015). “A Neural Conversational Model.” ICML Deep Learning Workshop. [link] Zhang, Y., et al. (2020). “DIALOGPT: Large-Scale Generative Pre-training for Conversational Response Generation.” ACL. [link] Three Roles Modern chatbot systems are usually built around three roles:
System: defines the assistant’s overall behavior and persona User: what the user says Assistant: what the model replies Chatbots follow the system role first, so you can use it to lock in specific behavior.
## example messages = [ {'role':'system', 'content':'You are an assistant that speaks like Shakespeare.'}, {'role':'user', 'content':'tell me a joke'}, {'role':'assistant', 'content':'Why did the chicken cross the road'}, {'role':'user', 'content':'I don\'t know'} ] Context Context: all the messages across the three roles that the chatbot needs in order to generate its next response.
Managing context well is one of the core engineering challenges in building a chatbot system — how do you make good use of the conversation history without it getting out of hand?
Key paper:
Bae, S., et al. (2022). “Keep Me Updated! Memory Management in Long-term Conversations.” EMNLP. [link]

https://www.coursera.org/learn/chatgpt-prompt-engineering-for-developers-project/home/welcome

Prompt engineering is the practice of designing and refining the input you give a large language model so it produces the output you actually want. It took off after GPT-3 came out, and it’s basically the bridge between what a user wants and what the model can do.

Key papers:

  • Brown, T. B., et al. (2020). “Language Models are Few-Shot Learners.” NeurIPS. [link] — the GPT-3 paper, the first to really demonstrate the potential of prompt engineering
  • Wei, J., et al. (2022). “Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models.” NeurIPS. [link]

1. Prompting Principles

Principle 1: Write clear and specific instructions

Clarity and specificity are the two things that matter most when writing a prompt. Vague instructions tend to produce unpredictable outputs, while specific ones noticeably improve output quality.

RAG RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) combines information retrieval with text generation — it pulls in an external knowledge base to make an LLM’s answers better.
Foundational papers:
Lewis, P., et al. (2020). “Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks.” NeurIPS. [paper] — the paper that started RAG Guu, K., et al. (2020). “REALM: Retrieval-Augmented Language Model Pre-Training.” ICML. [paper] Izacard, G., & Grave, É. (2021). “Leveraging Passage Retrieval with Generative Models for Open Domain Question Answering.” EACL. [paper] — a different take on RAG 1. Context Window What it is The context window is the maximum amount of text an LLM can read and reason over in a single pass.
Foundational paper:
Dai, Z., et al. (2019). “Transformer-XL: Attentive Language Models Beyond a Fixed-Length Context.” ACL. [paper] — early work on breaking past a fixed context length It usually has to fit:
the user’s question conversation history the system prompt retrieved documents whatever the model has generated so far All of that together has to stay under the model’s token limit.
Key things to know Anything over the limit gets truncated The model can only “see” what’s inside the window Window size directly affects: how long a document the model can handle how much material a RAG system can stuff in at once Context windows across mainstream models:
Model Context Window GPT-3.5 4K / 16K tokens GPT-4 8K / 32K tokens GPT-4 Turbo 128K tokens Claude 3 200K tokens Gemini 1.5 Pro 1M+ tokens 2. Token What it is A token is the basic unit a model works with when processing text.
Foundational papers:
Sennrich, R., Haddow, B., & Birch, A. (2016). “Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units.” ACL. [paper] — BPE, the basis for most modern tokenizers Kudo, T., & Richardson, J. (2018). “SentencePiece: A simple and language independent subword tokenizer.” EMNLP. [paper] A token can be:
a whole word a subword a fragment of a character Key things to know Model limits are almost always counted in tokens Cost scales directly with token count Different languages tokenize at different efficiencies (Chinese is usually more token-efficient than English) Rough rule of thumb:
English: about 4 characters = 1 token Chinese: about 1-2 characters = 1 token 3. Embedding What it is An embedding turns text into a numeric vector that represents its meaning.
Foundational papers:
Mikolov, T., et al. (2013). “Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space.” ICLR. [paper] — the original Word2Vec paper Pennington, J., Socher, R., & Manning, C. D. (2014). “GloVe: Global Vectors for Word Representation.” EMNLP. [paper] Devlin, J., et al. (2018). “BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding.” NAACL. [paper] — pioneered context-dependent embeddings Reimers, N., & Gurevych, I. (2019). “Sentence-BERT: Sentence Embeddings using Siamese BERT-Networks.” EMNLP. [paper] — Sentence-Transformers Sentences with similar meaning end up closer together in vector space.
Key things to know Embeddings show up in:
semantic search document retrieval recommendation systems clustering Common embedding models:
OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002 / text-embedding-3 Cohere Embed BGE (Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence) E5 (Microsoft) 4. Vector Search What it is Vector search finds relevant content by comparing vector similarity instead of matching keywords.
Foundational papers:
Johnson, J., Douze, M., & Jégou, H. (2019). “Billion-scale similarity search with GPUs.” IEEE Transactions on Big Data. [paper] — the Faiss vector database Malkov, Y. A., & Yashunin, D. A. (2020). “Efficient and robust approximate nearest neighbor search using Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs.” TPAMI. [paper] — the HNSW algorithm Common similarity measures:
Cosine similarity: $\cos(\theta) = \frac{A \cdot B}{|A| |B|}$ Dot product: $A \cdot B$ Euclidean distance: $|A - B|$ How it compares to traditional search Traditional search Vector search Keyword matching Semantic matching Exact match Ranked by similarity Can’t handle synonyms Understands semantic closeness 5. RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) What it is RAG is an AI system design pattern: retrieve external knowledge first, then generate the answer.
Foundational papers:
Lewis, P., et al. (2020). “Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks.” NeurIPS. [paper] Gao, Y., et al. (2023). “Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey.” arXiv. [paper] — a survey of the field The basic flow:
User question → vector retrieval → relevant documents found → LLM generates the answer Two flavors of RAG architecture Foundational paper:
Lewis, P., et al. (2020) laid out two variants: RAG-Sequence: uses the same set of retrieved documents for the whole generation RAG-Token: lets each generated token draw on a different document Why it’s useful Stays current without retraining the model Cuts down on hallucination, since answers are grounded in retrieved facts Plugs straight into a company’s own knowledge base Answers can be traced back to their source 6. Chunking What it is Chunking means breaking a long document into smaller pieces so it can be embedded and retrieved.
Foundational paper:
Lyu, C., et al. (2024). “Chunking Strategies for RAG.” arXiv. [paper] Why it’s necessary:
documents are usually too long to process as a whole embeddings work best when the content stays focused on one topic the context window is finite 7. Chunk Size What it is Chunk size is how many tokens go into each piece.
Typical ranges:
300–800 tokens for general use 100–300 tokens for Q&A 1000+ tokens when you need to understand a long document as a whole The trade-off Chunk Size Upside Downside Too large Full context preserved Semantics get diluted, retrieval gets less accurate Too small Tightly focused semantics Context gets lost, information gets fragmented 8. Overlap What it is Overlap means adjacent chunks share some content with each other.
The point: avoid cutting a sentence or a key piece of information right down the middle.
Typical setting: 10%–20%
Example:
Chunk 1: [0-500 tokens] Chunk 2: [400-900 tokens] # 100 tokens overlap Chunk 3: [800-1300 tokens] # 100 tokens overlap 9. Sliding Window What it is A sliding window is a chunking approach where neighboring chunks overlap partially with each other.
Foundational paper:
Liu, J., et al. (2022). “Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts.” arXiv. [paper] — looks at how the position of information inside a long context affects the model Advantages:
context isn’t lost less chance of a hard information break 10. Semantic Chunking What it is Semantic chunking splits text based on where the meaning shifts, rather than at a fixed token count.
Reference:
Loman, T., & Tekman, B. (2023). “Semantic Chunking for RAG.” [reference] Basic method:
Split by sentence Embed each sentence Compute similarity between neighboring sentences Start a new chunk once similarity drops below a threshold Why it helps:
keeps semantic units intact improves retrieval precision 11. Hybrid Chunking What it is What real systems tend to use: structural splitting + a token cap
Flow:
Split by headings/paragraphs → if over the length limit → split by sentence → add overlap Why it’s a good default:
stable and predictable respects natural semantic boundaries balances structure against length 12. Vector Database What it is A vector database stores embeddings and searches them for similarity efficiently.
Foundational papers and systems:
Johnson, J., Douze, M., & Jégou, H. (2019). “Faiss: A library for efficient similarity search.” [paper] Pinecone: a commercial vector database Weaviate: an open-source vector database Milvus: an open-source vector database [GitHub] Chroma: a lightweight vector database What it does: finds the closest matches out of a huge pool of vectors, fast.
Core techniques:
HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) IVF (Inverted File Index) PQ (Product Quantization) 13. Retrieval What it is Retrieval is the step that finds the most relevant document chunks from the vector database.
Flow:
User question → embedding → vector search → Top-K chunks Common choices: Top-3 / Top-5 / Top-10
Retrieval strategies:
Dense retrieval: based on vector similarity Sparse retrieval: based on keywords (e.g. BM25) Hybrid retrieval: combines both Foundational papers:
Robertson, S., & Zaragoza, H. (2009). “The Probabilistic Relevance Framework: BM25 and Beyond.” Foundations and Trends in IR. — the BM25 algorithm Karpukhin, V., et al. (2020). “Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering.” EMNLP. [paper] — DPR 14. Re-ranking What it is Re-ranking takes the retrieved results and sorts them again to push the more relevant ones to the top.
Foundational papers:
Nogueira, R., & Cho, K. (2019). “Passage Re-ranking with BERT.” arXiv. [paper] Nogueira, R., et al. (2020). “Document Ranking with a Pretrained Sequence-to-Sequence Model.” EMNLP. [paper] Flow:
Vector retrieval Top-20 → re-ranker model → Top-3 → LLM answers What it buys you: better retrieval precision, less irrelevant content getting through.
Common re-ranker models:
BGE Re-ranker Cohere Re-rank Cross-Encoder models 15. Hallucination What it is Hallucination is when a model generates something that sounds plausible but is factually wrong.
Foundational papers:
Maynez, J., et al. (2020). “On Faithfulness and Factuality in Abstractive Summarization.” ACL. [paper] Zhang, Y., et al. (2023). “Siren’s Song in the AI Ocean: A Survey on Hallucination in Large Language Models.” arXiv. [paper] Ji, Z., et al. (2023). “Survey of Hallucination in Natural Language Generation.” ACM Computing Surveys. [paper] Common causes:
the right document just isn’t retrieved not enough context an ambiguous prompt the model’s knowledge is out of date Ways to reduce it:
ground the model with RAG ask the model to cite its sources give it an explicit “I don’t know” option verify across multiple passes 16. Debugging a RAG System The usual order to check things in:
The user’s query (is it actually clear?) The Top-K chunks retrieved (did it find anything relevant?) The re-ranking output (is the ordering right?) The prompt (are the instructions clear?) The LLM itself (is it actually capable enough for the task?) Where problems tend to come from, in practice:
~80% from retrieval ~15% from the prompt ~5% from the model’s own capability Debugging tools:
LangSmith Arize Phoenix Weights & Biases 17. The Full RAG Pipeline Documents ↓ Chunking ↓ Embedding ↓ Vector Database (storage) ↓ Retrieval (Top-K) ↓ Re-ranking ↓ LLM generates the answer Wrapping Up The whole point of RAG, in one line:
Get the LLM the most relevant knowledge it can fit into a limited context window, so it can give an accurate answer.
Where the real optimization work happens:
chunking strategy embedding quality retrieval accuracy re-ranking prompt design

Transformer: From First Principles to a Product Lens 📚 Why does the Transformer matter so much? The Transformer architecture came out of Vaswani et al.’s 2017 paper “Attention Is All You Need.” It changed NLP completely and is now the backbone behind every major LLM — GPT, BERT, LLaMA, you name it.
The core idea: drop CNNs and RNNs entirely and rely only on the attention mechanism to capture dependencies across a sequence. That single move solved two problems at once:
Parallelism: RNNs process tokens one at a time; attention lets you process the whole sequence at once, which speeds up training enormously Long-range dependencies: RNNs/LSTMs tend to lose the signal over long sequences (vanishing gradients); attention doesn’t have that problem 🏗️ Part 1: The Overall Architecture 1.1 Encoder-decoder structure The Transformer follows the classic Seq2Seq encoder-decoder pattern:
Encoder: turns the input sequence (say, a sentence in the source language) into a continuous representation Made of N identical layers stacked on top of each other (N=6 in the original paper) Each layer has a multi-head self-attention sublayer plus a feed-forward sublayer Decoder: generates the target sequence based on what the encoder produced Also N identical layers stacked together Each layer has masked multi-head self-attention, encoder-decoder attention, and a feed-forward sublayer The masking: makes sure that when the decoder predicts position i, it can only see outputs before position i — otherwise it would be cheating by looking at the answer 1.2 Core components at a glance Component What it does What’s new about it Self-attention Captures relationships between any two positions in a sequence Global, and fully parallel Multi-head attention Looks at the sequence from several angles at once Multiple subspaces learned in parallel Positional encoding Gives the model a sense of word order Attention alone has no notion of position Feed-forward network Applies a non-linear transform at each position Adds expressive power Residual connections Wire the input straight through to the output Keeps deep networks from degrading Layer normalization Stabilizes the output distribution at each layer Faster, more stable convergence 🔍 Part 2: The Core Mechanisms 2.1 Self-attention The idea: let every word in a sequence look directly at every other word and figure out, dynamically, how relevant each one is.
How it works: Input representation: each input word $x_i$ gets turned into an embedding vector Building Q, K, V: three trainable weight matrices $W_Q, W_K, W_V$ project the input into Query, Key, and Value vectors Attention scores: take the dot product of a Query against every Key — this tells you how much the current position should attend to each other position Scale and normalize: divide by $\sqrt{d_k}$ (otherwise large dot products push the gradients toward zero), then run it through Softmax to get weights Weighted sum: use those weights to combine the Values into the final output The formula: $$ \text{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V $$
Why split into Q, K, V? Query: “what is this position looking for” Key: “what can this position offer” (a label or index) Value: “the actual content this position contributes once it’s attended to” Why three separate roles? It cleanly separates responsibilities — the Key decides how much attention a position gets, the Value decides what it hands over once attended to, and the Query decides what to look for. That’s a lot more expressive than cramming everything into a single vector.
2.2 Multi-head attention The idea: instead of looking at a sentence with one pair of eyes, use several pairs of “expert eyes” that each look at it from a different angle at the same time.
How it’s done:
Project Q, K, V into $h$ smaller subspaces ($h$ is the number of heads — 8, 12, whatever) Compute attention independently in each subspace Concatenate all the heads’ outputs and pass them through an output projection $W^O$ The formula: $$ \text{MultiHead}(Q,K,V) = \text{Concat}(\text{head}_1, \dots, \text{head}_h)W^O $$ $$ \text{head}_i = \text{Attention}(QW_i^Q, KW_i^K, VW_i^V) $$
Why it helps:
Division of labor: different heads end up specializing in different things — syntax, semantics, coreference, etc. More capacity: catches dependencies at different granularities Parallel-friendly: maps perfectly onto GPU compute A fun fact: nobody tells each head what to specialize in. That division of labor emerges on its own during training, purely from the data. Researchers can visualize what a head learned afterward, but they can’t prescribe it in advance.
2.3 Positional encoding Why bother? Self-attention has no built-in sense of order — shuffle the words in a sentence and you’d get the exact same output.
The fix: inject position information into the embeddings.
The sine/cosine scheme from the original paper: $$ PE_{(pos, 2i)} = \sin\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}}\right) $$ $$ PE_{(pos, 2i+1)} = \cos\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}}\right) $$ where $pos$ is the position, $i$ is the dimension index, and $d_{\text{model}}$ is the hidden size.
Why this design works well:
Values stay in $[-1, +1]$, so they don’t overwhelm the word embedding’s semantics It extrapolates to sequences longer than anything seen in training It naturally encodes relative position too ($PE_{pos+k}$ can be written as a linear combination of $PE_{pos}$) Where things have moved since: a lot of newer models (LLaMA, RoBERTa) use learned absolute positional embeddings or rotary position embeddings (RoPE) instead.
2.4 Feed-forward network Every Transformer layer includes a two-layer fully connected network: $$ \text{FFN}(x) = \max(0, xW_1 + b_1)W_2 + b_2 $$
A few things worth noting:
Applied independently at each position, with shared parameters The inner dimension is usually 4x wider (e.g. $d_{\text{model}}=512$, $d_{ff}=2048$) The ReLU non-linearity is what adds expressive power here One finding worth flagging: making this layer wider tends to help model performance.
2.5 Residual connections and layer normalization Stacking six or more layers deep creates training-stability problems, and these two tricks are what keep it from falling apart.
Residual connections What they solve: network degradation — past a certain depth, adding more layers can actually hurt performance instead of helping.
How it works: $$ \text{output} = \text{LayerNorm}(x + \text{Sublayer}(x)) $$
Why it works:
It gives gradients a “highway” straight back to earlier layers The network can learn an identity mapping, so a useless extra layer at worst does nothing rather than hurting things Borrowed directly from ResNet Layer normalization What it solves: vanishing/exploding gradients, so training stays stable.
How it works: normalize across all the features of a single sample using its mean and variance: $$ \text{LN}(x) = g \cdot \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma} + b $$ where $g$ and $b$ are learned scale and shift parameters, and $\mu$, $\sigma$ are the mean and standard deviation.
Two variants:
Post-norm: the original setup — normalize after the residual add Pre-norm: what most modern models use — normalize before the sublayer, which makes deep networks easier to train 📊 Part 3: A Closer Look at the Key Concepts 3.1 Hidden dimension ($d_{\text{model}}$ / hidden_size) What it is: the size of the “mental canvas” the model uses internally — how many numbers represent each word inside the model.
An analogy:
Small hidden dim (128-256): a pocket notebook — room for the essentials only Medium (768-1024): a regular desk — enough space to think things through properly Large (4096+): a full studio — room to really stretch out Why it matters: hidden dimension drives both how expressive the model is and how expensive it is to run. The bulk of a Transformer layer’s parameters scale with $d_{\text{model}}$ squared.
3.2 Attention heads What they are: the parallel units inside multi-head attention, each learning its own pattern of attention within a smaller subspace ($d_{\text{model}}/h$).
How many heads models typically use:
BERT-base: 12 layers, 12 heads BERT-large: 24 layers, 16 heads GPT-3: 96 layers, 96 heads LLaMA: 32/40/80 layers, 32/40/64 heads depending on size A more recent trick: Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) lets multiple heads share the same Key-Value projections, which shrinks the KV cache a lot at inference time with barely any quality loss (used in LLaMA 2/3).
3.3 Number of layers What it means: how “deep” the information refinement goes. Every layer gives the word vectors one more round of talking to each other in context.
The trade-off:
More layers: better at abstract reasoning, but needs more data, longer training, and more memory Fewer layers: trains fast, deploys easily, but struggles with complex tasks A rule of thumb: performance scales as a power law with layer count, hidden dimension, and data size together.
3.4 What the model’s weights actually are What’s inside the weights:
The attention projection matrices ($W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O$) The feed-forward weight matrices ($W_1, W_2$) Layer norm’s scale and shift parameters ($g, b$) The word embedding matrix Why are these files so huge? It comes down to parameter count × numeric precision:
FP32: 4 bytes per parameter FP16/BF16: 2 bytes per parameter INT8: 1 byte per parameter Formula: file size ≈ parameter count × bytes per parameter.
Example: LLaMA 3 70B stored in FP16 ≈ $70B \times 2 \text{ bytes} = 140\text{GB}$
Where do the weights come from? They’re learned through gradient descent and backpropagation on massive amounts of data — nobody hand-writes them.
🧮 Part 4: Estimating Parameter Counts 4.1 Parameter count for a single layer Component Formula Notes Embedding layer $V \times d_{\text{model}}$ $V$ is vocabulary size Multi-head attention $4 \times d_{\text{model}}^2$ Q/K/V projections (×3) + output projection (×1) Feed-forward network $2 \times d_{\text{model}} \times d_{ff}$ usually $d_{ff} = 4 \times d_{\text{model}}$ Layer norm $2 \times d_{\text{model}}$ two LN ops per layer (scale + shift) 4.2 Estimating the total Per layer ≈ $4d_{\text{model}}^2 + 8d_{\text{model}}^2 = 12d_{\text{model}}^2$ (assuming $d_{ff}=4d_{\text{model}}$)
Total model size ≈ $L \times 12d_{\text{model}}^2 + V \times d_{\text{model}}$ ($L$ = number of layers, $V$ = vocab size)
Sanity check with LLaMA 7B ($d_{\text{model}}=4096, L=32, V=32000$):
$32 \times 12 \times 4096^2 + 32000 \times 4096 \approx 6.4B + 0.13B = 6.53B$ — close enough to the “7B” name.
4.3 Estimating training cost The core formula: $C \approx 6PD$
$C$: total training compute (FLOPs) $P$: number of parameters $D$: training data size (tokens) Rule of thumb: a compute-optimal model roughly satisfies $D \approx 20P$
🚀 Part 5: From Pre-training to a Usable Model 5.1 Pre-training Goal: get the model to pick up general language patterns and world knowledge.
How: run either autoregressive language modeling (predict the next word) or masked language modeling (fill in the blank) on a huge pile of unlabeled text.
What you get: a base model that’s great at continuing text, but hasn’t been taught to follow instructions or match human preferences yet.
5.2 Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) Goal: teach the model to follow instructions and hold a conversation.
Data: high-quality, human-written instruction-response pairs.
In essence: a supervised task where the model learns to reproduce the “correct” answer.
5.3 RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) Goal: get the model’s outputs to better match human preferences — safe, helpful, harmless.
The pipeline:
Humans rank several model outputs by preference A reward model is trained to learn those preferences Reinforcement learning (e.g. PPO) is used to fine-tune the SFT model against that reward model 5.4 Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) Full fine-tuning is too expensive for large models, so a family of cheaper alternatives showed up:
LoRA: inject low-rank adapters and only train those Adapters: small trainable modules inserted between layers Prefix tuning: optimize a continuous prompt vector instead of the model weights 🔧 Part 6: Compression and Speed Deploying a big model means dealing with efficiency, and there are a few standard tools for that:
6.1 Quantization The idea: represent weights and activations with lower precision (INT8, INT4, etc.)
Two flavors:
Post-training quantization (PTQ): quantize after training, no retraining needed Quantization-aware training (QAT): simulate quantization error during training — better results, but more expensive Payoff: half the model size (FP16 → INT8) and faster inference
6.2 Pruning The idea: remove redundant attention heads, FFN layers, or individual weight connections that don’t matter much.
Two approaches: structured pruning (drop whole heads/layers) vs. unstructured pruning (drop individual weights)
6.3 Knowledge distillation The idea: train a small “student” model to mimic a large “teacher” model’s output distribution.
Why it helps: the student doesn’t just learn the right answer — it learns the teacher’s “way of thinking” via soft labels.
Where it’s used: shrinking cloud-scale models down to run on phones and IoT devices.
6.4 Parameter sharing The idea: share parameters across different layers.
Example: ALBERT cuts parameter count dramatically by sharing parameters across layers.
💡 Part 7: A Product Manager’s View of the Transformer 7.1 Key tradeoffs when picking a model Dimension What it means for the product The question to ask Hidden dimension The model’s “mental bandwidth” How big a canvas does this task need? Number of layers How deep the reasoning goes How many reasoning steps does the task take? Number of heads Size of the “expert panel” How many angles need to be covered at once? Parameter count Ceiling on capability, and on cost What size can the budget actually support? 7.2 Cost vs. capability Training cost ≈ $6 \times \text{parameters} \times \text{data size}$ Inference memory ≈ $1.2 \times \text{parameters} \times \text{bytes per parameter}$ (at inference time) Training memory: weights + gradients + optimizer state — typically 3-4x what inference needs 7.3 A rough decision checklist What’s the task complexity? Simple classification? Complex reasoning? Creative generation? What are the resource constraints? Cloud or on-device? Latency budget? Cost budget? Where do you start? A general-purpose model API, or an open model you can fine-tune? What’s the data plan? How much labeled data do you need, and how good does it have to be? How will you evaluate it? Model metrics vs. actual user experience metrics. 7.4 Where a model’s capability actually comes from Data: the scale, diversity, and quality of the pre-training data sets the ceiling on what the model can know. Architecture: the Transformer and its variants are what make parallel computation and long-range dependency modeling practical at this scale. Alignment: SFT and RLHF are what bend the model’s behavior toward what people actually want. References Vaswani et al. (2017). Attention Is All You Need Devlin et al. (2019). BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding Brown et al. (2020). Language Models are Few-Shot Learners Hoffmann et al. (2022). Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models Touvron et al. (2023). LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models Hu et al. (2022). LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models Sanh et al. (2019). DistilBERT, a distilled version of BERT: smaller, faster, cheaper and lighter

Transformer: From First Principles to a Product Lens

📚 Why does the Transformer matter so much?

The Transformer architecture came out of Vaswani et al.’s 2017 paper “Attention Is All You Need.” It changed NLP completely and is now the backbone behind every major LLM — GPT, BERT, LLaMA, you name it.

The core idea: drop CNNs and RNNs entirely and rely only on the attention mechanism to capture dependencies across a sequence. That single move solved two problems at once:

  • Parallelism: RNNs process tokens one at a time; attention lets you process the whole sequence at once, which speeds up training enormously
  • Long-range dependencies: RNNs/LSTMs tend to lose the signal over long sequences (vanishing gradients); attention doesn’t have that problem

1. Comparing the mainstream payment methods 1. Business-to-business cash transfer How it works: an initiated transfer from a bank counter or corporate online banking, or a payment through a bank’s fund-splitting system with a receipt.
Limits: large transfers are possible. Anything above RMB 50,000 goes through the PBOC’s large-value payment system, which doesn’t run on weekends and holidays, and can be affected accordingly (on weekdays it runs from 20:30 the previous evening through 17:15 the same day).
Time to arrive: usually settles promptly.
How the platform confirms receipt: finance staff can check the bank account manually, match a unique code in the remittance memo back to the order automatically, or, if it goes through a bank fund-splitting system, get near-real-time confirmation.
2. Gateway payment The customer is sent to a unified checkout page hosted by a third-party payment company or bank, then redirected to their bank’s own online banking to pay.
Limits: depend on the card type and its security tier.
Bank coverage: depends on how many banks the checkout provider has partnered with.
3. Aggregated / QR code payment There are two flows: customer-scans (the shopper’s app opens the camera and scans the merchant’s QR code) and merchant-scans (the shopper shows their payment code for the merchant to scan). E-commerce web pages use the customer-scans flow.
A QR code from an aggregated payment provider usually supports several payment methods at once (WeChat, Alipay, etc.), which makes integration easier for the merchant.
A single-channel code from one payment company — a WeChat or Alipay collection code, say — only works with that one app, but the tradeoff is a more stable, better experience.
4. Third-party app payment This launches a third-party payment app directly. The top three in China are WeChat Pay, Alipay, and UnionPay QuickPass. WeChat has broad coverage offline; Alipay leans on the Taobao ecosystem and keeps pushing tap-to-pay innovations to hold its ground against WeChat; QuickPass, as the “national team” option, has decent reach too, helped by consumption subsidies and its one-stop bank card management. Others — JD Pay, LianLian Pay, and so on — trail the top three in scale but hold their own advantages in specific scenarios.
Bank coverage: essentially complete, and all support balance and credit-based payment. WeChat currently focuses on personal payments and doesn’t support binding a corporate account; Alipay lets you create a business account and pay against it.
5. Mobile quick pay (H5) This binds a bank card through a payment channel’s H5 page. It’s not used much these days — most major payment companies offer this form, but H5 pages carry more security risk than an in-app flow, and the experience is worse (users have to log in repeatedly).
6. Card-based quick pay The platform integrates with a payment company; once a user binds their card on the platform, they can just pick a card to pay.
Some channels support password-free payment. That shifts some risk-control responsibility onto the platform, but the tradeoff is a smoother, faster payment experience.
Bank coverage: depends on how many banks the provider has partnered with.
7. Wallet balance payment This means acquiring a payment license, or partnering with a third-party payment company, to offer a wallet feature that lets users top up and pay from balance.
The platform needs risk controls around top-ups, payments, and withdrawals. This is good for the user experience and helps build stickiness.
8. Buy-now-pay-later credit lines Well-known examples include Huabei, JD Baitiao, and Meituan Yuefu. A financial institution extends the user a credit line to pay with, and for consumer users, the platform often subsidizes interest for the first month. This can meaningfully boost user stickiness — some B2B clients in particular care a lot about cash flow, and offering payment terms builds a tighter working relationship — but it also demands solid credit assessment and risk control.
9. Monthly settlement (running a tab) A merchant lets a specific customer buy on credit or sign a monthly settlement agreement, keeps its own ledger, and asks the customer to settle up periodically. If a platform runs its own retail business, it may build features for this too. These transactions aren’t backed by any third-party guarantee and don’t necessarily go through the platform at all — it’s typically used between a merchant and a customer they know well and work with closely.
10. Digital RMB Functionally equivalent to cash. It’s available today through payment apps and QR code scanning, though usage is still fairly low.
11. Pay-on-behalf The buyer creates an order and shares a pay-on-behalf checkout link with someone else to pay. The payment methods offered on that shared checkout page need to account for the payer’s identity, device environment, and similar factors.
12. Buy now, pay later (BNPL) A low credit bar, typically with small limits that don’t get reported to the PBOC’s credit system. The platform guarantees the transaction and charges the merchant a service fee; on the consumer side, users typically need to set up direct debit from a bound bank card. My own take is that this lowers the friction of the purchase decision without feeling as heavy as a credit product like Huabei.

content:
I’ve recently been working on some anti-fraud and anti-money-laundering projects, and it’s given me a much more concrete sense of how telecom fraud and money laundering actually work. E-commerce platforms are an easy target for criminals, and as a product manager you have to design with that risk in mind from the start — if crime ends up happening on your product, the best case is you feel terrible about it, and the worst case is regulatory penalties. Under China’s “dual penalty” system, that liability now runs from the platform all the way down to the individuals responsible. Fighting this kind of crime is everyone’s job.
Reference material Why do top-up-and-withdraw platforms keep turning into money-laundering tools for scammers? //zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/151289531
Full text of China’s Anti-Telecom and Online Fraud Law //zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/560714960
Designing the risk control system An e-commerce platform’s account system typically has a few core functions: account opening, stored value, transactions, and withdrawals. Each function needs guardrails scoped to its business case from day one, and once it’s live you need to keep thinking about how it could be abused, monitor user data, catch abnormal behavior quickly, and back it up with limits, alerts, and blocking.
At account opening, KYC needs to be done properly — don’t open the door to users who aren’t your intended audience, and if your account system has multiple tiers, map users to the right tier strictly rather than loosely. Don’t loosen these controls just to keep future feature changes flexible or to chase faster growth — you need to weigh business needs against security at design time, and chasing a growth metric while ignoring security can backfire badly.
For stored value, you need to decide which payment channels can fund it. Credit cards generally should be blocked, and B2B transfers into a personal wallet-style account need handling that matches what kind of virtual account the platform actually is. Beyond that: does this user actually need to hold a balance? How much do they typically top up? When do they usually do it? These patterns all need research and matching controls — capping top-up amounts, blocking certain users from topping up at all, disallowing balance payment for certain business lines, flagging top-ups at unusual hours, and so on.
Transaction monitoring is one of an e-commerce platform’s core jobs. Since the platform has already vetted and screened both buyers and sellers on the way in, what’s really left is verifying that a given transaction is genuine. From a fund-splitting standpoint, “transaction” is a broader concept than just a purchase — any transfer from account A to account B counts, and transfers can show up outside the normal buying flow too. You need to check that a transaction makes sense — not just for ordinary purchases, but for any transfer-like movement between user accounts or between merchant accounts. Transactions that come from edge-case business scenarios and don’t map to an actual purchase should be tightly restricted — support the narrowest version of that use case and block anything beyond it. For transactions tied to actual purchases, check frequency and amount to catch buyers and sellers colluding on fake transactions to launder money through the platform, and where needed, verify the paying user’s identity to guard against account takeover or account trading.
A refund back to the original payment method is generally low-risk. Withdrawal is one of only two ways money leaves a user’s account (setting aside platform-side deductions like fees) — so however many issues slipped through earlier, if this last line of defense holds, you avoid an actual loss of funds. Withdrawals need their own security checks, plus tight controls on where the money can go. Withdrawal amount, frequency, and how fast it settles all need risk rules. If it’s a B2B platform where withdrawals aren’t very frequent, manual review is a perfectly reasonable option.
Bottom line: risk control has to guard against competitors, insiders, and unknown bad actors all at once — you can’t design for just one threat. Different bad actors use different tactics. And as a product person, if a piece of business carries a lot of inherent risk, the best move is often to just not build it; if you have to, think hard about which version of it carries the least risk.
