Notes from working through Cross-Border E-Commerce Payment and Settlement, my starting point for getting into cross-border payments.
A few basic concepts Foreign exchange (FX) Foreign exchange is a claim held by a country’s monetary authorities — the central bank, currency management bodies, exchange stabilization funds, and the treasury — in the form of bank deposits, treasury bills, and short- and long-term government securities, that can be drawn on to cover a balance-of-payments deficit. It covers foreign currency itself, foreign-currency deposits, foreign-currency securities (government bonds, treasury bills, corporate bonds, stocks), and foreign-currency payment instruments such as drafts, bank certificates of deposit, and postal savings certificates.
Broad definition All of a country’s assets denominated in foreign currency — essentially the movement of money across borders and the conversion of one country’s currency into another’s to settle cross-border credit and debt. In practice this is the claim that a country’s monetary authorities (central bank, currency management bodies, exchange stabilization funds, and treasury) hold in the form of bank deposits, treasury bills, and government bonds, usable when the country runs a balance-of-payments deficit.
Narrow definition Payment instruments denominated in a foreign currency, generally accepted internationally, and usable to settle cross-border debts. To qualify, an asset needs three properties: payability (it must be a foreign-currency-denominated asset), availability (the claim must be redeemable abroad), and convertibility (it must be freely exchangeable into other payment instruments).
Floating exchange rate regimes The level of the franc’s exchange rate wasn’t set by speculators, by the trade balance, or even by adventures in the Ruhr — it was set by how much of their own income French taxpayers were willing to hand over to France’s rentiers. — Keynes
One basic anchor for an exchange rate is purchasing power parity. Say an egg costs RMB 1 in China and USD 0.2 in the US — then 1 RMB should trade for about 0.2 USD. If instead the two currencies traded 1:1, RMB 1 would still buy one egg at home, but converted to USD it would buy several eggs in America. People would rush to swap RMB for USD to buy American eggs, RMB would flow out to the US and eggs would flow into China. Domestic egg sellers would lose the market, domestic prices would stop being competitive, capital would keep leaving, and meanwhile demand for American eggs would outstrip supply, pushing US prices up until ordinary Americans couldn’t afford eggs — China would be buying up America’s eggs with cash it printed. Neither side wants that outcome, which is exactly why an exchange rate exists: to keep the domestic market stable and cross-border trade fair by converting between the two currencies.
Of course reality ran the other way round. We used to have gold as the yardstick; then the US came to dominate the world and the dollar replaced gold, with international settlement done in dollars — letting the US print money to buy eggs from the rest of the world. In 1973 the dollar-centered fixed exchange rate system finally broke down, and countries and regions moved one after another to floating rates. In practice, exchange rates are also shaped by trade protection, financial markets, and politics. To reduce our reliance on the dollar, we’ve been pushing RMB settlement, and we’ve also built a more stable exchange rate regime of our own.
China runs a managed float based on market supply and demand, referencing a basket of currencies — a managed floating exchange rate system. Each day the PBOC (People’s Bank of China) publishes the RMB’s rate against the dollar and other major currencies based on the prior day’s interbank FX market pricing, and banks quote their own rates within the band the PBOC sets around that midpoint. The PBOC itself is also a major player in the interbank FX market and can buy or sell FX to steer the rate as part of its monetary policy.
Traditional cross-border payment methods Remittance Remittance runs on commercial credit — the bank is just an agent carrying out an instruction; whether payment actually happens depends on the buyer honoring the contract.
Mail transfer: the remitting bank sends a mail transfer order to the receiving bank, which then pays out to the beneficiary. Wire transfer (telegraphic transfer): the remitting bank sends an encrypted cable or telex to the receiving bank to release the funds. Remittance by draft: the payer actively pays the beneficiary using a draft, promissory note, check, or similar instrument. Collection Collection is the reverse of remittance — the documents move opposite to the funds. The exporter draws a bill of exchange on the importer and instructs its own bank to collect payment through the importer’s branch or correspondent bank.
Collection also runs on commercial credit: the bank acts strictly on the seller’s instructions, and whether payment is made depends entirely on the buyer’s creditworthiness.
Clean collection: typically used for small amounts, advance payments, installments, or ancillary trade charges — the financial document isn’t accompanied by a commercial document. Documentary collection: the financial instrument travels together with the commercial documents. Letter of Credit (L/C) An L/C runs on bank credit. It’s independent of the underlying sales contract (a self-sufficient instrument) and detached from the goods themselves (a purely document-based transaction) — the issuing bank carries the primary obligation to pay.
Newer cross-border payment methods Traditional cross-border trade was mostly large-ticket B2B business settled through banks. As the internet took off, B2B, C2C cross-border e-commerce, and small-ticket B2B trade all grew fast, and a wave of new cross-border payment methods emerged alongside them. Domestically, most of these are run by third-party payment providers holding a payment business license from the PBOC and an approval from SAFE (China’s foreign exchange regulator) to run cross-border e-commerce FX payment pilots.
Some of the mainstream new-style cross-border payment options:
Domestic: Alipay, WeChat Pay, LianLian Pay, PingPong
International: PayPal, Western Union, WebMoney (widely used across Russian-speaking countries, Japan, Europe, and the US)
These providers mainly earn money from payment processing fees and payment solutions, plus some non-recurring income such as FX spreads.
Compared with traditional methods, the new-style cross-border payment options bring lower fees, simpler payment flows, faster settlement, and the ability to handle the high-concurrency traffic that platforms see.
How third-party providers implement payment Cross-border e-commerce platforms typically integrate multiple payment channels and route between them — much the same as domestic payments.

Wrapping up what to prepare for when you’re new to a job, and the mistakes I made so I don’t forget them.
1. Get your tools set up
Find out what software the company runs on day to day. If IT already has it installed for you, great. If it’s something you’ve never used, learn the basics when you have a spare moment, or just ask a colleague.
2. Learn how the place actually works
Get a feel for the org chart, the general workflow — does product development run through an internal system, through docs, or through some third-party tool — and how the different departments coordinate with each other.
Get a rough sense of the engineering org too: their general skill level, their main tech stack, if you can find that out.
3. Meet your coworkers
No need to rush getting close to everyone — you’re not going to remember all the names on day one anyway, and honestly the more important thing here is for them to remember you. But do remember the people you’ll be working closely with, and make a good first impression with them.
Get a read on the team’s vibe and pace, and your manager’s working style.
If you get the chance, take a colleague or your manager out for a meal — it’s a good way to learn more about the company and what’s expected of you.
4. Get up to speed on the business*
A few things worth memorizing outright: the company’s main business lines, its values, the internal jargon, the key metrics, the main competitors, and the market and policy landscape. Most companies have a deck or doc covering this; ask around for anything it doesn’t cover.
Products worth actually using: for anything owned by your own team, walk through the main flows yourself and use it hands-on — a mind map really helps organize your thinking here. Do the same with the main competitors so you understand what’s similar and what’s different.
For the product you’re personally taking over, use every feature, hit every state, and draw out the flow diagrams as you go. Whatever’s unclear, go ask the person who was handling it before. If you’re confused about something or a feature seems overly complex, pull up the old requirement docs if the company kept them — that’s also a good way to learn the company’s conventions for writing requirement docs.
For the business your product touches, try to experience it firsthand if you can — or at minimum, understand the basics: current pain points, where it’s headed, what its core strengths or value are, and its business model.
Build a feel for the data — pull the relevant event-tracking and reporting data and actually look at it, so you have real numbers in your head, not just impressions.
5. Ground rules for writing requirement docs
Everyone’s busy, so don’t reinvent the wheel — if there’s already a mature product doing this, or a writeup online, go read it. It’ll also help you handle pushback later.
Explain the background of the requirement — it makes it easier for engineering to understand, and it shows you’re not just making up requests on a whim.
Spell out the entry point for the feature — engineering might be new to this part of the product too and won’t necessarily know where it lives.
Spell out every state and every transition — engineers often won’t catch these on their own, even when the logic seems obvious to you. Write it out anyway.
For anything involving numbers or options, be explicit: min/max values, defaults, format requirements, and how those formats should actually be implemented. This is the baseline, not optional.
Spell out how to handle edge cases — for anything you can reasonably foresee going wrong, write down how to prevent it or handle it. Every single step needs this kind of thinking.
And — this one matters a lot — always include diagrams.
6. How to carry yourself
Stay humble, keep a low profile, and be polite to both your colleagues and engineering. When something’s frustrating day to day, put yourself in the other person’s shoes — be mindful of tone and timing when you ask someone for something. Everyone’s stretched thin.
Always confirm requirements explicitly with engineering and QA — make sure they actually know what’s expected. Don’t just write the doc and consider your job done.
Once development is finished, test it yourself. Once it’s live, go check the actual result yourself too.

content:
When you’re digging into what users actually need, it’s rarely something concrete and explicit. There’s the old Ford line — “if I’d asked people what they wanted, they’d have said a faster horse” — but once you get to actually building the product, you still have to land on something concrete: specific features that satisfy the underlying need. So what I mean by “requirement analysis and management” here is the whole chain: start from a surface-level ask, dig into the real need underneath it, evaluate it, land on a specific solution, and hand that off to engineers and designers to turn into an actual product. B2B and B2C products differ quite a bit in how this plays out.
Software requirements split roughly into functional and non-functional. Functional requirements are the concrete things the software needs to do — registration, rollback, and so on. Non-functional requirements cover things like stability and how well the system handles high concurrency. Requirements need priority and they need numbers attached. The important ones get built first, and they need to be quantified — you tell engineering “response time needs to be under X ms,” not “make it faster.”
1 Requirement Analysis 1.1 Who’s Involved Users — the people who actually use the software. Clients — the people who commission the company to build it. Market analysts — people who study the market and simulate the client’s perspective. Leadership — the people issuing top-down direction.
1.2 Requirement Changes Requirements change — because the original analysis missed something, because the client’s environment or business process shifted, or because the market moved. That’s not necessarily a bad thing: yes, it means more work, but it can also push the product forward. Two things help you handle it well. First, any change should go through a review and comparison before it gets implemented — don’t just rubber-stamp whatever the client asks for or whatever idea comes up; push back on the wilder ideas so you’re not doing pointless work. Second, when you’re writing the requirement doc in the first place, think in terms of modules and future growth, understand the business details fully, sketch out the product’s overall structure up front, and leave room to handle both the expected and the unexpected. Thinking it through early makes the later work go much more smoothly. Take a registration flow: beyond the happy path, you need to cover every failure mode and edge case — account already exists, password too weak, required field left blank, invalid format, bot protection, verification email never arrives, the link in the email doesn’t open, and so on.
1.3 Where Requirements Come From Leadership direction: goals handed down from the top. A PM’s job is to evaluate those goals and, once they’re confirmed, break them down and prioritize them. Industry knowledge: a PM needs to track where the industry is heading — new technology and new concepts bring new requirements, or clash with existing ones, and it’s on the PM to judge that using their domain knowledge. For example, the AI wave might mean your product needs new AI-related features or an upgrade to existing ones; if a competitor gets there first with some advantage and markets it heavily, that’s a real competitive threat. User base: requirements users raise directly, or that come out of analyzing them. A product’s users are rarely a uniform group — different roles, different cultures, different org structures produce different needs, and you have to sort through that carefully to build something that actually fits. Operating environment: changes in user scale, or regional infrastructure like network conditions, can force the product to adapt. Organizational environment: for B2B products especially, policy, company culture, workflows, and org structure often drive custom requirements. 1.4 Gathering Requirements Experience it yourself — sit in on the actual business work, use the product yourself. Workshops — bring the relevant people together, plan the discussion flow and questions ahead of time, and keep good notes. Ask domain experts — talk to people who own that part of the business. Brainstorming — one-on-one or in a group, cast a wide net, then filter down to what’s actually useful. Surveys — send questionnaires to users. Desk research — go through internal documents and data to find requirements hiding in there. 1.5 Models for Requirement Analysis 1.5.1 The Kano Model Kano splits requirements into five tiers:
Basic (must-be): what users consider table stakes. Missing it tanks satisfaction; adding more of it barely moves the needle. Performance (expected): the more you deliver, the happier users are, and vice versa. Excitement (delighters): features users didn’t expect. Deliver them and users are thrilled; skip them and satisfaction doesn’t drop. Indifferent: users barely notice either way. Reverse: most users actively don’t want this — give it to them anyway and they’re unhappy. (Airing a boys’-love drama on state TV would obviously backfire — and would never happen in the first place.) When prioritizing, satisfy basic needs first, then performance needs, then delighters — and skip indifferent or reverse ones. Sometimes you’ll still build something indifferent, just to round the product out or keep a client happy. In user research, people tend to voice performance needs on their own; basic needs and delighters are the ones you have to dig out and infer yourself, because users take the former for granted and can’t imagine the latter. Over time, delighters and performance needs tend to sink down into basic needs — camera quality used to wow people; now a flagship phone with a bad camera is simply unacceptable.
1.5.2 Maslow’s Hierarchy — the Y-Model Maslow’s hierarchy points at the deep, underlying human needs. When a user raises a request, the Y-model lets you trace it back: what goal is the user actually trying to reach by getting this? What motivation sits underneath that goal, and which level of Maslow’s hierarchy does it map to? From there you design the feature to serve that human need directly. Generally, features that map to the lower rungs of the hierarchy are more foundational and more utility-driven — think maps, food delivery apps — and those needs should be prioritized.
① is the user’s stated request — the starting point, the surface, the first layer of depth: what need, in what scenario, for what user, doing what. ② is the goal and motivation behind that request — the second layer: why is the user actually asking for this, and what’s the underlying motivation? When thinking through the user’s goal, you also have to weigh the company’s and the product’s goals. ③ is the product feature — the solution you land on after digging through the layers above, described in a way the implementation team can act on. ④ is the human need — Maslow’s need, the third and deepest layer: values, human nature itself.
The real value of the Y-model is that it won’t let you skip step ② and jump straight from ① to ③. Going deeper into the user’s actual need helps you: avoid being misled by fake requirements, resolve conflicting requirements, uncover goals you hadn’t seen, hold onto what’s constant about human nature, and find openings even in a mature, crowded market.
//zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/123364228
1.5.3 User Journey Maps Requirements tend to come in scattered. A user journey map turns them into a story and a picture — pulling everything together to help shape a coherent experience design. Mapping out the journey step by step also makes requirements easier to spot, and layering in the user’s mood or cost at each step surfaces pain points in the product or service flow.
A user journey map needs a clearly defined user, the business scenario, the actions/mindset/emotions at each step, the touchpoints and channels (when and where the user interacts with the product or service), and the insights and ownership (what’s going wrong at a given step, and who’s responsible for it).
http://www.woshipm.com/user-research/1089015.html
summary: When you’re digging into what users actually need, it’s rarely something concrete and explicit. There’s the old Ford line — “if I’d asked people what they wanted, they’d have said a faster horse” — but once you get to actually building the product, you still have to land on something concrete: specific features that satisfy the underlying need. So what I mean by “requirement analysis and management” here is the whole chain: start from a surface-level ask, dig into the real need underneath it, evaluate it, land on a specific solution, and hand that off to engineers and designers to turn into an actual product. B2B and B2C products differ quite a bit in how this plays out.
title: Notes on Requirement Analysis and Management

1 Why Bother with Competitive Analysis 1. Better decisions. Understanding competitors’ products helps you position your own — and steer clear of the strongest players so you don’t wander into a red ocean. It lowers the risk of getting your bets wrong.
2. Learning from others. Studying what makes a competitor’s product strong lets you build more deliberately: take what works, absorb their strengths, and use it to sharpen your own edge.
3. Early warning. Keeping an eye on how competitors evolve means you catch disruptive substitutes or new policy changes early, so you can react before they hurt you.
2 Product Lifecycle and Competitive Analysis 3 The General Process Get clear on the goal — why are you doing this analysis Pick your competitors Decide what dimensions to analyze Gather information Organize and analyze it Write up the summary report 3.1 Getting Clear on the Goal Why is this product doing a competitive analysis in the first place? What stage of its lifecycle is it in? What are the current problems and challenges — can competitive analysis actually help solve them? What’s the underlying purpose of doing this? What are the concrete objectives (the purpose is reached by hitting a set of specific objectives)? These objectives might include: supporting a decision, early market warning, or learning from competitors. For example: figuring out whether this product has a future and is worth building, and how to make money from it; seeing how a successful competitor did it so you can do something similar and grab market share; or tracking the market regularly to catch risks early and understand why your share is shrinking so you can course-correct. What’s the deliverable — a standalone report, or part of a business plan / project proposal? 3.2 Picking Competitors The selection criteria depend on your goal:
For decision support or risk warning, look at brand competitors, category competitors, and substitutes — screened by market share, whether they’re backed by a big company, user feedback, and cross-industry substitutes. For learning from others, look at brand competitors, category competitors, and reference products — screened by market share, cross-industry references, and category pioneers. Once you’ve shortlisted candidates, narrow them down again based on your actual situation — your goal, your own market share, how competitive the market is, what stage your product is at. In practice you usually end up analyzing around 3.
Don’t pick competitors by gut feeling — you’ll miss important ones.
3.3 Choosing What to Analyze You can look at a product from two angles: the product’s own perspective and the user’s. The product angle covers what actually determines success or failure — supply chain, manufacturing, tech stack — things users never see. The user angle is what users actually weigh when choosing between products, which for near-identical products is often just price. You can gather this user-side view through surveys and interviews.
Which dimensions matter depends on your goal, the product category, and its key success factors. Focus on what actually decides the outcome: is this product won on technology or on design? Is it B2C or B2B — the two call for very different lenses. If you’re analyzing an enterprise finance system, visual design usually isn’t worth much attention.
3.4 Gathering Information Collect thoroughly, but know when to stop.
Common data sources: Baidu Index, Umeng, Alibaba Index, Tencent Big Data, Analysys, iResearch, CNNIC, TalkingData, Alexa, Qimai Data Patent search: Patent Search and Analysis
3.5 Organizing and Analyzing Don’t just collect information — process it. Don’t just list findings — actually analyze them. Processing means summarizing, categorizing, combining, and checking reliability.
Common analysis methods:
3.5.1 Comparison Methods Checkbox comparison, scored comparison, descriptive comparison (see $APPEALS).
3.5.2 Matrix Analysis Identify the key competitive factors and use them to think through positioning.
3.5.3 Competitor Tracking Matrix Time-consuming, so it’s usually reserved for core products. For products that ship fast, frequent small updates, roll them up and analyze the major releases instead.
3.5.4 Feature Breakdown Get a full picture of what a competitor’s product is made of so nothing slips through the cracks. Ways to do it: (1) break it down by nav menu, (2) by user flow, (3) by interaction pattern, (4) by reading the product manual.
3.5.5 Digging into the Real Need Dig past the surface to find the deeper need a competitor’s product is actually satisfying — that’s where a better solution comes from. Needs sit at three levels: solution-level → problem-level → human-level. Say a user needs a chair — that’s a solution-level statement. Is a chair really what they need? It’s just one way to solve their actual problem. Maybe what they actually want is to rest — that’s the problem-level need. Push one layer deeper: why do they want to rest? In an extreme example, maybe they want to live longer so they have more time with family and more time to enjoy life — that’s the human-level need underneath it all. Once you’ve found that, you can build toward it directly. Forget the chair — build an “ion recovery chair” that claims to extend your life… if the user has a strong enough underlying need, they might drop the chair entirely and buy your product instead.
In practice, don’t stop after asking “why” once or twice — keep pushing until you hit the real reason. It’s basically Toyota’s 5 Whys.
3.5.6 PEST Analysis A product sits inside three nested layers: macro environment → industry environment → company environment → product. PEST analysis looks at the macro environment — building a product means working with the tide, not against it, and macro forces can make or break a product or even a company. Combine PEST with Porter’s Five Forces and you get the opportunities and threats half of a SWOT. PEST works well as a group brainstorm: have people from different roles list macro factors independently, merge the similar ones, then vote to pick the top 3–5.
Beyond the classic PEST factors there’s also law, demographics, ecology, and others — pull them in as needed. And since the outside world moves fast, PEST analysis needs to be refreshed regularly.
3.5.7 Porter’s Five Forces Porter’s Five Forces looks at the industry environment — how attractive and profitable the industry is. How strong each of the five forces is determines how competitive the industry gets, which in turn determines how sustainable high margins are. Strong supplier bargaining power makes it hard to push costs down; strong buyer bargaining power makes it hard to push margins up.
3.5.8 SWOT Analysis Works like a checklist — laying out factors across all four quadrants to help shape a competitive strategy. Strengths and weaknesses are internal; opportunities and threats are external. Strengths and weaknesses should come out of actual comparison with competitors, not guesswork. And don’t just list everything — filter and distill to what’s actually relevant to your analysis goal and dimensions. Doing a proper SWOT usually pulls in several of the methods above — comparison, matrix analysis, PEST, Porter’s Five Forces.
3.6 Writing the Summary The summary should be value-driven and built around the original goal of the analysis. It typically needs to land on a competitive strategy and action plan. A few frameworks help with that:
3.6.1 SWOT-Based Strategy 3.6.2 Porter’s Three Generic Strategies Cost leadership: cut production and operating costs to win on price and earn above-average industry margins. Works best for companies doing manufacturing at scale. Differentiation: build something different from competitors and win users on unique value. Tools for this include the strategy canvas and the eliminate-reduce-raise-create grid. Works best for companies with a broad product line. Focus: also called niche strategy — serve one specific user group or market segment well. Works best in a narrow market. 3.6.3 Other Competitive Strategies 4 Tools for Competitive Analysis 4.1 Lean Canvas The lean canvas is for mapping out and analyzing a product’s business model. Ash Maurya introduced it in Running Lean — it helps a PM think more holistically, make better calls, and build a full-picture view of the product from a systems and business standpoint. Use it for product planning, breaking down a competitor’s business model, or as a discussion tool.
Lean canvas tools and methods:
4.2 Competitor Canvas The competitor canvas is basically the MVP of a competitive analysis report. It’s a quick way to get started and validate your direction early, so you don’t end up writing a full report that misses the point.
4.3 Strategy Canvas The strategy canvas helps you map out a “blue ocean” strategy — finding untapped markets through differentiation. In practice: plot a value curve with competitive factors on the x-axis.

Tensors Tensor = container
Tensors are the foundation everything in modern machine learning sits on. At its core a tensor is just a container — usually of numbers, occasionally of strings, though that’s rarer. Think of it as a bucket of numbers.
A 0-D tensor is a scalar; a 1-D tensor is a vector; a 2-D tensor is a matrix; a 3-D tensor (and up) is what you use for shared data storage — things like color images.
One-hot vectors One-hot encoding is used for categorical labels. For example, (cat, dog, mouse) maps to (1,0,0) for cat, (0,1,0) for dog, and so on. Encoding discrete features this way makes distance calculations between features much more sensible.
The softmax function Softmax does two things: it runs the model’s raw scores through an exponential function so they all come out non-negative, and then it normalizes them so all the resulting probabilities add up to 1.
//blog.csdn.net/lz_peter/article/details/84574716
Cross-entropy For single-label multi-class classification, p(x) is the ground-truth label — with one-hot encoding this is just 0 or 1 — and q(x) is the predicted probability for that class. Using cross-entropy as the loss function, the smaller the value, the closer the model’s predictions are to reality.
In single-label multi-class problems, the probabilities across all classes sum to 1. In multi-label binary classification they don’t — cross-entropy there is computed per class (as a binary decision), and then you sum the binary cross-entropy across classes for a given sample.
//blog.csdn.net/tsyccnh/article/details/79163834
Euclidean space Euclidean space is just the formal, generalized version of the physical space we’re used to — extended from n ≤ 3 dimensions to any finite n dimensions.
Euclidean geometry is the plane and solid geometry you learned in school — where, notably, parallel lines stay the same distance apart everywhere.
The geometry you learn in school is normally 2D or 3D (which is why cosine similarity, distances between points, and inner products all get introduced in low-dimensional space first). Once you generalize the rules you learned in those low-dimensional spaces to any finite n dimensions, spaces that satisfy those definitions are what we call Euclidean space. What Euclidean space really defines is the inner product, distance, and angle — the same concepts from middle school geometry. Once that clicks, the formal math definition makes a lot more sense.
//www.zhihu.com/question/27903807/answer/699570097
Vanishing and exploding gradients Hidden layers closer to the output have larger gradients, so their parameters update quickly and converge fast.
Hidden layers closer to the input have much smaller gradients, so they update slowly and stay close to their random initial state.
In the four-layer hidden network shown above, the first layer trains almost 100x slower than the fourth!
That’s the vanishing gradient problem. The opposite case — where gradients in earlier layers grow through training and gradients in later layers grow exponentially — is called the exploding gradient problem.
Bottom line: in a deep network, gradients can get pretty unstable.
//www.cnblogs.com/yangmang/p/7477802.html
Batch size The batch size mainly determines the direction of descent — the bigger the batch, the more accurate that direction.
It comes down to the size of your dataset. When the dataset is small, you can just use the whole thing as your batch, which gives you the most accurate descent direction. When it’s large, a relatively small batch can still get you a global learning rate similar to using the full dataset — so the real trade-off is learning effectiveness versus efficiency versus how much memory your machine actually has, and you want to max out both effectiveness and efficiency at once.
What do you gain from increasing batch size within a reasonable range?
Better memory utilization, and more efficient parallelization for large matrix multiplications. Fewer iterations needed to finish one epoch, so you process the same amount of data faster overall. Generally, a larger batch size gives a more accurate descent direction and less training oscillation. Past a certain point, though, increasing batch size further stops helping efficiency, and the descent direction barely changes anymore.
//blog.csdn.net/starzhou/article/details/53692248
Learning rate Pseudocode for gradient descent:
Repeat until convergence: {ωj = ωj − λF(ωj)/ωj}
λ is the learning rate. Too small, and optimization can be painfully slow; too large, and you risk overshooting the optimum and converging to a local minimum instead.
For more on picking a good learning rate, adjusting it dynamically, normalization, etc., see:
//www.cnblogs.com/mazhujun/p/9633576.html
